 1.1 Produits tensoriels topologiques et espaces nucléaires (1949- 1953) The Ph.D. Thesis [1949-53]1 situates Grothendieck among the most brilliant mathematicians of his generation. The history is well known2 , according to which the contestant young man who had passed the year 1948-49 in the Séminai- re Cartan is sent by an annoyed Cartan in 1949 to Nancy, where his men- tors Schwartz and Dieudonné asign him fourteen open problems to calm his frenzy. Some months later, he has solved them all, and possesses, according to Schwartz’s testimony, many results which would suffice for multiple papers. The Thesis, a development of those researches, is defended in 1953 (February 28th, jury composed by Henri Cartan (Président), Laurent Schwartz (Rapporteur) and Gustave Choquet (Examinateur)), and published in 1955 by the American Mathematical Society. Tensorial products and nuclear spaces (introduced by Grothendieck) are studied at the core of the work. In some subsequent accounts of the Thesis, Grothendieck emphasizes a characterization of nuclearity through a soft coin- ˆ cidence of projectivity (ˆ) and injectivity (ˆ) (later denoted (ˇ)), that is, E is ˆ ≈ E ⊗F nuclear if and only if E ⊗F ˇ for all F locally convex (or, alternatively, for all F Banach ([1952a, 100], [1952b, 196]). The article’s inventiveness, mathematical and symbolical, constitutes one of the most achieved and harmonious texts of Grothendieck’s output, and may be recommended as a first entry to his world. After finishing his Thesis, it is hard to find a job in France for the young stateless, and Schwartz and Dieudonné help him to get a postdoc in São Paulo4 . In the first year, between March and October 1953, he produces his monograph on topological vector spaces5 [1953d] and the Résumé [1953c], yielding another period of splendour. The Résumé is submitted a year later to the Boletim da Sociedade de Matemática de São Paulo6 and published in that journal in 1956. The second year in São Paulo will be instead a time of crisis (the only one reckoned by Grothendieck in his mathematical life7 ), which will propel him to algebraic geometry (see Subsection 1.3 below). A natural continuation of the Thesis [1949-53], the Résumé provides a new understanding of classes (not yet called “categories”) of Banach and Hilbert spaces, from a triple perspective attentive to inequalities between tensorial norms, analytic structures and algebraic factorizations. “Grothendieck’s theorem, past and present”. In: Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 49 (2012), pp. 237–323. 4 space can be characterized as being simultaneously a subspace of type L and a quotient of type C, that is, simultaneously a λ and γ space. The methodological strategy of the Résumé [1953c] is fascinating: (i) de- scribe comparable canonical norms, (ii) transform those norms, (iii) cover the full spectrum thanks to a structural hierarchy. Those three general levels pos- sess various sublevels of understanding: (A) following Bourbaki, we have (i) order, (ii) topology, (iii) algebra; (B) semiotically, we have (i) semantics, (ii) syntactics, (iii) pragmatics; (C) phenomenologically, we have (i) separation, (ii) continuity, (iii) entrelacs9 ; (D) musically, we have (i) theme, (ii) variations, (iii) fugue. In particular, at level (i) we can recognize one of Grothendieck’s major obsessions. In fact, from his Thesis until his generalized proof of Riemann-Roch, passing through the creation of abelian categories, Grothendieck detected ubiq- uitous appearances of projectivity and injectivity in many mathematical regions: projective and injective products (Thesis [1949-53]), projective and injective norms (Résumé [1953c]), existence of enough injectives in abelian categories with a generator and infinitude axioms in order to reconstruct homology from derived functors (Tôhoku [1955-56]), inductive sub-specializations (= “spatial- izations”) of the generalized Riemann-Roch proof in the projective and injective cases (Rapport Riemann-Roch [1955-57]).  The abstract and the concrete, the universal and the particular, categorical reason and mathematical heart, become all necessary to nurture mathematical imagination. Mathematics has to explore all possible worlds, be- yond mere actuality, but, on the other hand, many of her greatest achievements occur when a general architecture illuminates an actual conjecture. The back- and-forth between types and archetypes, elevated to a method in Grothendieck’s work, helps to understand the irreducible complexity of mathematical thought. 36 Grothendieck Works Grothendieck, A. Il représente la majorité des travaux de Grothendieck, de 1949 à 1991 et donne un exemple du réseau scientifique (relations et échanges de documentation) d’un mathématicien au sommet de la recherche internationale dans la deuxième moitié du XXème siècle.
Son père, Alexander Schapiro (dit Sascha), né en Ukraine d’une famille juive, est anarchiste. En 1949, Grothendieck débute sa thèse à Nancy sous la direction de Jean Dieudonné et Laurent Schwartz (médaillé Fields l’année suivante). En quelques mois, il résout quatorze problèmes sur lesquels ces deux mathématiciens de renom butaient. Il fréquente alors le groupe de réflexion mathématique Bourbaki, dans lequel il sera très actif entre 1955 et 1960. En 1953, il présente pour la thèse sa théorie des produits tensoriels topologiques et espaces nucléaires. Grothendieck ne peut cependant pas occuper un poste dans la fonction publique. En effet, né en Allemagne, il n’en demeure pas moins apatride. De 1950 à 1958, il occupe donc la fonction de chercheur rattaché au Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS). Grothendieck est d’abord reçu à l’université de São Paulo comme professeur invité (1952-1954) puis à l’université de Lawrence (Kansas) où il développe une théorie de topologie algébrique et d’algèbre homologique (1955). Après un séjour à l’université de Chicago, il obtient une bourse du CNRS et rentre à Paris en 1956.

Résumé des résultats essentiels dans la théorie des produits tensoriels topologiques et des espaces nucléaires

Grothendieck, Alexander

Annales de l'Institut Fourier, Tome 4 (1952), pp. 73-112

L’auteur donne un résumé des résultats essentiels de son travail “Produits tensoriels topologiques et espaces nucléaires” (à paraître dans Memoirs of the Am. Math. Soc.), en essayant de faire ressortir les idées directrices. Soient E et F deux espaces localement convexes, on définit d’abord deux topologies naturelles sur E\otimes F, qui donnent des complétés E\widehat{\otimes }F et E\widehat{}\widehat{\otimes }F, qu’on explicite dans divers cas importants, et dont on élucide les propriétés algébrico-topologiques, notamment à l’égard de la notion de produit tensoriel d’applications linéaires continues. Le dual de E\widehat{\otimes }F est l’espace des formes bilinéaires continues sur E\times F, tandis que le dual de E\widehat{}\widehat{\otimes }F est formé des formes bilinéaires continues sur E\times F pouvant s’exprimer par certaines intégrales, et appelées pour cela formes bilinéaires intégrales.
